concepts: Scalar triple product and vector triple product
Dot and cross product of vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$ and $\vec b=\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$. If $\vec c$ is a vector such that $\vec a\cdot\vec c=11$, $\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec c)=27$ and $\vec b\cdot\vec c=-\sqrt3\,|\vec b|$, then $|\vec a\times\vec c|^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Since $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$, $\vec b\times(\vec a\times\vec c)=-3\vec a$, which fixes $|\vec b||\vec a\times\vec c|$ from its sine and cosine parts.
solution: $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k,\ \vec b=\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$, so $\vec a\cdot\vec b=1+2-3=0$ ($\vec a\perp\vec b$). Also $|\vec b|=\sqrt3$, so $\vec b\cdot\vec c=-\sqrt3\cdot\sqrt3=-3$.
Given $\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec c)=27$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$.
Expand: $\vec b\times(\vec a\times\vec c)=\vec a(\vec b\cdot\vec c)-\vec c(\vec b\cdot\vec a)=-3\vec a$.
Let $\theta$ be the angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec a\times\vec c$. Then $|\vec b||\vec a\times\vec c|\sin\theta=|\vec b\times(\vec a\times\vec c)|=|-3\vec a|=3\sqrt{14}$.
Also $|\vec b||\vec a\times\vec c|\cos\theta=\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec c)=27$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Resolve $\vec c$ along the orthogonal triad $\vec a,\vec b,\vec a\times\vec b$ and use $|\vec a\times\vec c|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec c|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec c)^2$.
solution: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$, so $\vec a,\ \vec b,\ \vec n=\vec a\times\vec b=-5\hat i+4\hat j-\hat k$ are mutually perpendicular, with $|\vec a|^2=14,\ |\vec b|^2=3,\ |\vec n|^2=42$.
$\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec c)=\vec c\cdot(\vec b\times\vec a)=-\vec c\cdot\vec n$, so $\vec c\cdot\vec n=-27$.
The components of $\vec c$ along the triad are $\vec c\cdot\vec a=11,\ \vec c\cdot\vec b=-3,\ \vec c\cdot\vec n=-27$.
Lagrange's identity: $|\vec a\times\vec c|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec c|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec c)^2=14\cdot29-121=285$.
Check: solving the three linear equations gives $\vec c=3\hat i-2\hat j+4\hat k$, with $|\vec c|^2=29$ and $\vec a\times\vec c=14\hat i+5\hat j-8\hat k$, so $|\vec a\times\vec c|^2=285$.

useful_results: Lagrange's identity: $|\vec u\times\vec v|^2=|\vec u|^2|\vec v|^2-(\vec u\cdot\vec v)^2$; it turns a cross-product length into dot products.
For $\vec a\perp\vec b$: $\vec b\times(\vec a\times\vec c)=\vec a(\vec b\cdot\vec c)$, so the vector triple product collapses to a multiple of $\vec a$.
If $\vec a,\vec b,\vec a\times\vec b$ are mutually perpendicular, any $\vec c$ is determined by its three dot products with them, and $|\vec c|^2=\sum\frac{(\vec c\cdot\vec e)^2}{|\vec e|^2}$.
$\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec c)=\vec c\cdot(\vec b\times\vec a)$ (cyclic invariance of the scalar triple product) converts a triple-product condition into a linear condition on $\vec c$.

questions.question: If $\vec a=2\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$, then the value of $\left|\hat i\times(\vec a\times\hat i)\right|^2+\left|\hat j\times(\vec a\times\hat j)\right|^2+\left|\hat k\times(\vec a\times\hat k)\right|^2$ is equal to _____ .
questions.key_idea: $\hat i\times(\vec a\times\hat i)$ is the part of $\vec a$ perpendicular to $\hat i$, so the three squares add up to $2|\vec a|^2$.
solution: $\hat i\times(\vec a\times\hat i)=(\hat i\cdot\hat i)\vec a-(\vec a\cdot\hat i)\hat i=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k-x\hat i=y\hat j+z\hat k$. $\quad$ (i)
Similarly $\hat j\times(\vec a\times\hat j)=x\hat i+z\hat k$. $\quad$ (ii)
and $\hat k\times(\vec a\times\hat k)=x\hat i+y\hat j$. $\quad$ (iii)
Required sum $=|y\hat j+z\hat k|^2+|x\hat i+z\hat k|^2+|x\hat i+y\hat j|^2=(y^2+z^2)+(x^2+z^2)+(x^2+y^2)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the third vector as $x\hat i+y\hat i$ (and the stem line as 'y j' with i/j mix-ups); the correct vector in (iii) is $x\hat i+y\hat j$. Only a typo; the value 18 is unchanged and correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $\hat e\perp(\vec a\times\hat e)$, $|\hat e\times(\vec a\times\hat e)|=|\vec a\times\hat e|$; then Lagrange's identity gives $|\vec a|^2-(\vec a\cdot\hat e)^2$.
solution: For a unit vector $\hat e$, $\hat e\perp(\vec a\times\hat e)$, so $|\hat e\times(\vec a\times\hat e)|=|\hat e||\vec a\times\hat e|=|\vec a\times\hat e|$.
Lagrange's identity with $|\hat e|=1$: $|\vec a\times\hat e|^2=|\vec a|^2-(\vec a\cdot\hat e)^2$.
Sum over $\hat e=\hat i,\hat j,\hat k$: $3|\vec a|^2-\left[(\vec a\cdot\hat i)^2+(\vec a\cdot\hat j)^2+(\vec a\cdot\hat k)^2\right]=3|\vec a|^2-|\vec a|^2=2|\vec a|^2$.
Check with components: the perpendicular parts are $(0,1,2),(2,0,2),(2,1,0)$ with squared lengths $5+8+5=18$.

useful_results: $\hat e\times(\vec a\times\hat e)=\vec a-(\vec a\cdot\hat e)\hat e$ is the component of $\vec a$ perpendicular to the unit vector $\hat e$; its squared length is $|\vec a|^2-(\vec a\cdot\hat e)^2=|\vec a|^2\sin^2\phi$.
For any orthonormal triad $\hat e_1,\hat e_2,\hat e_3$: $\sum|\vec a\times\hat e_k|^2=2|\vec a|^2$ (here $18$ for $|\vec a|^2=9$), because $\sum(\vec a\cdot\hat e_k)^2=|\vec a|^2$.
Similarly $\sum_k\hat e_k\times(\vec a\times\hat e_k)=2\vec a$, a handy identity for sums over $\hat i,\hat j,\hat k$.

concepts: Angle between a line and a plane
questions.question: Let $\theta$ be the angle between the planes $P_1:\vec r\cdot(\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k)=9$ and $P_2:\vec r\cdot(2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k)=15$. Let $L$ be the line that meets $P_2$ at the point $(4,-2,5)$ and makes an angle $\theta$ with the normal of $P_2$. If $\alpha$ is the angle between $L$ and $P_2$, then $\left(\tan^2\theta\right)\left(\cot^2\alpha\right)$ is equal to ______ .
questions.key_idea: The angle between a line and a plane is $\frac{\pi}{2}-$(angle with the normal), so $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta$.
solution: Normals: $\vec n_1=\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$ and $\vec n_2=2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$, each of magnitude $\sqrt6$.
$L$ makes the angle $\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$ with the normal of $P_2$, so the angle between $L$ and the plane is $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{\pi}{6}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Get $\tan\theta$ from $|\vec n_1\times\vec n_2|/(\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2)$ and use $\cot\alpha=\tan\theta$, so the product is $\tan^4\theta$ with no angle recognition.
solution: $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2=(\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k)\times(2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k)=3\hat i+3\hat j-3\hat k$, of magnitude $3\sqrt3$.
$\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2=3$, so $\tan\theta=\frac{|\vec n_1\times\vec n_2|}{\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2}=\sqrt3$.
The line makes angle $\theta$ with the normal, hence $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta$ and $\cot\alpha=\tan\theta$.
The point $(4,-2,5)$ does not matter: the answer depends only on the two angles.

useful_results: Angle between a line and a plane $=\frac{\pi}{2}-$ (angle between the line and the normal), so $\sin\alpha=\cos\theta$ and $\cot\alpha=\tan\theta$.
$\tan\theta=\frac{|\vec n_1\times\vec n_2|}{\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2}$ gives the angle between two vectors (or planes) without computing $\cos^{-1}$.
The angle between two planes equals the angle between their normals (taking the acute value); the position of a point on the line is irrelevant to an angle question.

concepts: Distance of a point from a plane
Locus of a point (sum of squared distances)
questions.question: Let $P$ be an arbitrary point having sum of the squares of the distances from the planes $x+y+z=0$, $lx-nz=0$ and $x-2y+z=0$ equal to $9$. If the locus of the point $P$ is $x^2+y^2+z^2=9$, then the value of $l-n$ is equal to _____.
questions.key_idea: Writing the locus and comparing coefficients with $x^2+y^2+z^2=9$ forces the cross term $xz$ to vanish, giving $l=n$.
solution: Let $P(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$. The sum of squared distances from the three planes is $9$: $\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}{\sqrt3}\right)^2+\left(\frac{l\alpha-n\gamma}{\sqrt{l^2+n^2}}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\alpha-2\beta+\gamma}{\sqrt{1+4+1}}\right)^2=9$.
But the locus is $x^2+y^2+z^2=9$. Comparing coefficients of $x^2$ and $zx$:
questions.correction_note: In the expanded locus the PDF gives the coefficient of $z^2$ as $\frac12+\frac{l^2}{l^2+n^2}$; it must be $\frac12+\frac{n^2}{l^2+n^2}$. It also omits the factor 2 in the $zx$ term (it writes $\alpha zx(\ldots)$ with the stray symbol $\alpha$ instead of $2zx(\ldots)$). Neither slip affects equations (1), (2) or the answer 0.

alternate_solutions.idea: The sum of squares of distances equals $x^2+y^2+z^2$ for all points exactly when the three unit normals are mutually perpendicular.
solution: The unit normals are $\vec u_1=\frac{(1,1,1)}{\sqrt3},\ \vec u_2=\frac{(l,0,-n)}{\sqrt{l^2+n^2}},\ \vec u_3=\frac{(1,-2,1)}{\sqrt6}$, and the sum of squared distances is $\sum(\vec u_k\cdot\vec r)^2=\vec r^{\,T}M\vec r$ with $M=\sum\vec u_k\vec u_k^{\,T}$.
Requiring $\vec r^{\,T}M\vec r=|\vec r|^2$ for all $\vec r$ means $M=I$, i.e. $U^TU=I$ for the matrix $U$ with rows $\vec u_k$; so the rows are orthonormal.
$\vec u_2\perp\vec u_1$: $l+0-n=0$; and $\vec u_2\perp\vec u_3$: $l-n=0$ (the same condition).

useful_results: For planes through the origin with unit normals $\vec u_k$, $\sum d_k^2=\vec r^{\,T}\left(\sum\vec u_k\vec u_k^{\,T}\right)\vec r$; this equals $|\vec r|^2$ for all $\vec r$ iff the three normals are mutually perpendicular (an orthonormal basis).
Distance of $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ from $ax+by+cz+d=0$ is $\frac{|ax_1+by_1+cz_1+d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$; the squares remove the modulus, so the locus is a quadric.
A normal $(l,0,-n)$ perpendicular to two other normals is a sign that it should be proportional to their cross product; here $(1,1,1)\times(1,-2,1)=(3,0,-3)\propto(1,0,-1)$, i.e. $l=n$.

concepts: Angle between a line and a plane
Point of intersection of a line and a plane
questions.question: Let the line $\ell:\ x=\frac{1-y}{-2}=\frac{z-3}{\lambda},\ \lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ meet the plane $P:\ x+2y+3z=4$ at the point $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$. If the angle between the line $\ell$ and the plane $P$ is $\cos^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{5}{14}}\right)$, then $\alpha+2\beta+6\gamma$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The line-plane angle $\phi$ satisfies $\sin\phi=\frac{|\vec d\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec d||\vec n|}$, which fixes $\lambda$ before the intersection is found.
solution: The line is $x=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-3}{\lambda}$, so its direction ratios are $(1,2,\lambda)$.
The normal of the plane $x+2y+3z=4$ has direction ratios $(1,2,3)$.
The angle $\phi$ between line and plane: $\sin\phi=\frac{|1+4+3\lambda|}{\sqrt{5+\lambda^2}\sqrt{14}}$.
A variable point of the line is $\left(t,\ 2t+1,\ \frac23t+3\right)$.
It lies on the plane: $t+2(2t+1)+3\left(\frac23t+3\right)=4\Rightarrow7t+11=4\Rightarrow t=-1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\cos\phi=\frac{|\vec d\times\vec n|}{|\vec d||\vec n|}$, which leads to a linear equation in $\lambda$ with no modulus or squaring.
solution: So $(\lambda-3)^2=5+\lambda^2$, which gives $-6\lambda+9=5$ and $\lambda=\frac23$ (the $\lambda^2$ terms cancel).
Substituting the point $(t,2t+1,\frac23t+3)$ in the plane gives $t=-1$, point $\left(-1,-1,\frac73\right)$, and $\alpha+2\beta+6\gamma=11$.

useful_results: Line-plane angle $\phi$: $\sin\phi=\frac{|\vec d\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec d||\vec n|}$ and $\cos\phi=\frac{|\vec d\times\vec n|}{|\vec d||\vec n|}$; the cross-product form often gives a linear equation because the $\lambda^2$ terms cancel.
Beware: the angle in the question is with the plane, so the dot product goes with $\sin$, not $\cos$ (a common trap when the angle is given as $\cos^{-1}$).
To meet a line and a plane, write the line in parametric form and substitute in the plane; one linear equation fixes the parameter.

questions.question: Let $\vec a=3\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$ and $\vec c=2\hat i-3\hat j+3\hat k$. If $\vec b$ is a vector such that $\vec a=\vec b\times\vec c$ and $|\vec b|^2=50$, then $\left|72-|\vec b+\vec c|^2\right|$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $|\vec a|=|\vec b\times\vec c|$ fixes $\sin\theta=\frac1{10}$, hence $\vec b\cdot\vec c=\pm33$, and $|\vec b+\vec c|^2=72+2\vec b\cdot\vec c$.
solution: $|\vec a|=|\vec b\times\vec c|$ with $|\vec a|=\sqrt{9+1+1}=\sqrt{11}$ and $|\vec c|=\sqrt{4+9+9}=\sqrt{22}$.
$|\vec b+\vec c|^2=|\vec b|^2+|\vec c|^2+2|\vec b||\vec c|\cos\theta=50+22+2\cdot5\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt{22}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{99}}{10}$ (PDF uses $\cos\theta>0$).
$\left|72-|\vec b+\vec c|^2\right|=|72-138|=66$. If $\cos\theta$ is negative, $|\vec b+\vec c|^2=72-66=6$ and $|72-6|=66$ again.

alternate_solutions.idea: Lagrange's identity $|\vec b|^2|\vec c|^2-(\vec b\cdot\vec c)^2=|\vec b\times\vec c|^2$ gives $\vec b\cdot\vec c$ directly, with no angle.
solution: Lagrange: $(\vec b\cdot\vec c)^2=|\vec b|^2|\vec c|^2-|\vec b\times\vec c|^2=1100-11=1089=33^2$, so $\vec b\cdot\vec c=\pm33$.
Consistency: $\vec a\cdot\vec c=6-3-3=0$, as it must be since $\vec a=\vec b\times\vec c\perp\vec c$.

useful_results: Lagrange's identity: $(\vec b\cdot\vec c)^2+|\vec b\times\vec c|^2=|\vec b|^2|\vec c|^2$; given any two of the dot product, cross product and the lengths, the third follows.

$\vec a=\vec b\times\vec c$ is solvable only if $\vec a\cdot\vec c=0$ (and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$); this is a quick consistency check, and then $\vec b$ is determined up to adding a multiple of $\vec c$.
$|\vec b\pm\vec c|^2=|\vec b|^2+|\vec c|^2\pm2\vec b\cdot\vec c$; the modulus in the question absorbs the sign ambiguity of $\cos\theta$ when only $\sin\theta$ is known.

concepts: Area of a triangle using vector product
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Let the co-ordinates of one vertex of $\triangle ABC$ be $A(0,2,\alpha)$ and the other two vertices lie on the line $\frac{x+\alpha}{5}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+4}{3}$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}$, if the area of $\triangle ABC$ is $21$ sq. units and the line segment $BC$ has length $2\sqrt{21}$ units, then $\alpha^2$ is equal to __________ .
questions.key_idea: Area $=\frac12\cdot BC\cdot h$ gives $h=\sqrt{21}$, the distance from $A$ to the line, computed as $\frac{|\vec{AP_0}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$.
solution: The line passes through $P_0(-\alpha,1,-4)$ with direction $\vec d=5\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$, $|\vec d|=\sqrt{38}$.
Area of $\triangle ABC=\frac12\cdot BC\cdot h$, where $h$ is the distance of $A$ from the line: $21=\frac12\cdot2\sqrt{21}\cdot h$, so $h=\sqrt{21}$.
$\overrightarrow{P_0A}=\alpha\hat i+\hat j+(\alpha+4)\hat k$ and $h=\frac{|\overrightarrow{P_0A}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$.
$\overrightarrow{P_0A}\times\vec d=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ \alpha&1&\alpha+4\\ 5&2&3\end{vmatrix}=(-2\alpha-5)\hat i+(2\alpha+20)\hat j+(2\alpha-5)\hat k$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's first line ends with $=21\sqrt{21}$ on the right-hand side; with area $21$ and $BC=2\sqrt{21}$ the correct right-hand side is $21$ (the next line, $\sqrt{21}\sqrt{38}$, is consistent with $21$ and not with $21\sqrt{21}$). It also writes the roots as '$\alpha=3$' without noting the rejected root $-\frac{29}{3}$ (not an integer). Answer 9 is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Pythagoras in the right triangle $A$, foot, $P_0$: $h^2=|AP_0|^2-\left(\overrightarrow{P_0A}\cdot\hat d\right)^2$, avoiding the determinant.
solution: $\overrightarrow{P_0A}\cdot\vec d=5\alpha+2+3\alpha+12=8\alpha+14$, so the squared length of its projection on the line is $\frac{(8\alpha+14)^2}{38}$.

useful_results: Distance of a point $A$ from the line through $P_0$ with direction $\vec d$: $h=\frac{|\overrightarrow{P_0A}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$, or $h^2=|P_0A|^2-\frac{(\overrightarrow{P_0A}\cdot\vec d)^2}{|\vec d|^2}$.
If two vertices of a triangle lie on a line, the area is $\frac12\cdot$(base on the line)$\cdot$(distance of the third vertex from the line); the positions of $B,C$ on the line do not matter.
Always apply the stated condition ($\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}$) to reject extra quadratic roots: here $-\frac{29}{3}$ is discarded.

concepts: Section formula and intersection of a line with a plane
Perpendicular from a point to a line and direction ratios
questions.question: The point of intersection $C$ of the plane $8x+y+2z=0$ and the line joining the points $A(-3,-6,1)$ and $B(2,4,-3)$ divides the line segment $AB$ internally in the ratio $k:1$. If $a,b,c$ ($|a|,|b|,|c|$ are coprime) are the direction ratios of the perpendicular from the point $C$ on the line $\frac{1-x}{1}=\frac{y+4}{2}=\frac{z+2}{3}$, then $|a+b+c|$ is equal to __________ .
questions.key_idea: The given line lies in the plane $8x+y+2z=0$, so the perpendicular from $C$ is perpendicular to both the line and the plane's normal.
solution: The line $\frac{x-1}{-1}=\frac{y+4}{2}=\frac{z+2}{3}$ has the general point $D(1-\lambda,\ -4+2\lambda,\ -2+3\lambda)$ and direction $(-1,2,3)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the line as $\frac{x-1}{-1}=\frac{y+4}{2}=\frac{z+2}{2}$ in the working (the denominator of $z$ should be $3$, as in the stem). Its next lines use the correct direction $(-1,2,3)$, so only the printed line is a typo; the answer 10 is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: The line lies in the plane $8x+y+2z=0$, so the perpendicular from $C$ is perpendicular to the plane's normal $(8,1,2)$ and to the line: take the cross product.
solution: Direction of the given line: $\vec d=(-1,2,3)$; normal of the plane: $\vec n=(8,1,2)$. $\vec d\cdot\vec n=-8+2+6=0$.
The point $(1,-4,-2)$ of the line satisfies the plane: $8-4-4=0$. So the whole line lies in the plane $8x+y+2z=0$.
$C$ is also in this plane, so the perpendicular from $C$ to the line lies in the plane and is perpendicular to $\vec n$ as well as to $\vec d$.
These are already coprime in magnitude, so $|a+b+c|=|-1-26+17|=10$, agreeing with the main solution (which gave the same ratios up to a factor $5$).

useful_results: If a line lies in a plane, the perpendicular from any point of the plane to that line lies in the plane, so its direction is $\vec n\times\vec d$ (perpendicular to the normal and to the line).
Foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to the line through $P_0$ with direction $\vec d$: $\lambda=\frac{(C-P_0)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}$ (here $\frac{11}{14}$).
Section formula: for $A$, $B$ and ratio $k:1$, $C=\frac{kB+A}{k+1}$; a plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=0$ meets $AB$ at $k=-\frac{\vec n\cdot A}{\vec n\cdot B}$ (here $-\frac{-28}{14}=2$).

concepts: Plane through a given line (family of planes)
Plane parallel to a line and distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: Let the equation of the plane passing through the line $x-2y-z-5=0=x+y+3z-5$ and parallel to the line $x+y+2z-7=0=2x+3y+z-2$ be $ax+by+cz=65$. Then the distance of the point $(a,b,c)$ from the plane $2x+2y-z+16=0$ is __________.
questions.key_idea: Use the family $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ and the parallelism condition $\vec n\cdot\vec d=0$ to fix $\lambda$.
solution: The plane passes through the line $x-2y-z-5=0=x+y+3z-5$, so its equation is $(x-2y-z-5)+\lambda(x+y+3z-5)=0$.
The direction of the line $x+y+2z-7=0=2x+3y+z-2$ is $(1,1,2)\times(2,3,1)=(-5,3,1)$.
The plane is parallel to this line, so the normal of (1) is perpendicular to $(-5,3,1)$: $-5(1+\lambda)+3(\lambda-2)+1\cdot(3\lambda-1)=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The plane contains the first line and is parallel to the second, so its normal is the cross product of the two direction vectors, and it passes through one point of the first line.
solution: Direction of the first line: $(1,-2,-1)\times(1,1,3)=(-5,-4,3)$; direction of the second: $(-5,3,1)$.
A point on the first line: put $z=0$, so $x-2y=5$ and $x+y=5$, giving $(5,0,0)$.
Plane: $13x+10y+35z=13\cdot5=65$, which matches the form $ax+by+cz=65$ with $(a,b,c)=(13,10,35)$.

useful_results: The plane through the line $P_1=0=P_2=0$ is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ (all such planes except $P_2=0$); the direction of the line $\{n_1\cdot r=d_1,\ n_2\cdot r=d_2\}$ is $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$.
A plane containing one line and parallel to another has normal $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$; the constant term then comes from one point of the first line.
The plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=c$ is parallel to a line with direction $\vec d$ iff $\vec n\cdot\vec d=0$; distance of a point from the plane is $\frac{|\vec n\cdot P-c|}{|\vec n|}$.
